title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 8
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a city literary narrative, an economics passage on pay for unpleasant work with a data table, a humanities essay on film sound effects, and paired science passages on light pollution), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, four passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Natural Science — paired passages A and B

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about 10 minutes per passage: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score (1–36).

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original short story. The narrator, now an adult, remembers a summer in Cairo when a broken leg kept him inside his family's flat.

[1] The summer I was twelve, I fell off a wall I had been told not to climb and spent the next two months with my leg in plaster, a prisoner on the fourth floor. My friends visited for the first week, then less often, and then the long holiday carried them off — to the sea, to their grandparents' villages, to football in the dusty lot behind the mosque. After that I had only the window.

[2] Our window looked across a narrow street to the roof of the building opposite, a flat, untidy place crowded with satellite dishes and a wooden shed on stilts. I had seen the shed all my life without wondering what it was. On my third evening alone, I found out. At the hour when the heat began to break, a heavy man in a vest climbed onto the roof, unlatched the shed, and the air above the street filled with wings.

[3] There were perhaps sixty pigeons. They burst out together, rose above the rooftops and began to circle, wide and then wider, wheeling as a single body that turned from grey to silver whenever it caught the sun. The man stood in the middle of the roof with a long bamboo pole, a scrap of red cloth tied to its end, and moved it slowly through the air like a conductor. When he whistled — two notes, the second higher — the whole flock swung round at once and came down out of the sky to settle around his feet.

[4] My mother told me that he was called Am Ragab and that he repaired pipes for half the district. To me he became something else. Every evening I arranged myself by the window half an hour early, my bad leg propped on a chair, and waited. I began to know the birds. There was a big dark one that always landed first, a pair that flew so close together they seemed to be tied, and one small white pigeon that never quite joined the others. It flew its own circles, a little lower and a little later, and it was always the last to come down.

[5] I worried about the white one. I decided that it was lost, or slow, or unwanted, and each evening I watched it with my heart in my throat until it landed. Once it did not come down at all before dark, and I lay awake imagining it alone over the city. The next evening it was there again, flying its lonely circles, and I was so relieved that I laughed out loud.

[6] It was around then that Am Ragab noticed me. Perhaps he had seen me for weeks; perhaps he had only just looked up. He lifted the pole and dipped the red cloth towards my window, the way he did when he wanted the birds to turn. I waved back, feeling foolish and delighted. After that he did it every evening.

[7] In the last week of August, the plaster came off. I went down four flights of stairs like an old man, crossed the street and climbed the six flights opposite, stopping on every landing. Am Ragab was waiting on the roof as if he had expected me. He did not seem surprised that I knew the birds; he seemed surprised only that I had taken so long to visit.

[8] I asked him about the white pigeon. He laughed and said it was the best bird he had. It flew apart, he explained, because it was watching for hawks, and it came down last because it would not land until the others were safe. "You thought it was the weakest," he said. "It is the one I trust."

[9] I asked him another question that had been bothering me: why the birds came back at all, when the whole sky was open to them. He shrugged, as if the answer were obvious. "Because here is where they are fed and where they sleep safely," he said. "I let them go every evening so that every evening they can choose to come home."

[10] I am older now than Am Ragab was then, and I live in another city. But I still cannot pass a flock of pigeons circling over the rooftops without looking for the one that flies a little apart.
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
c: A narrator recalls how, while stuck at home one summer, he grew attached to a neighbour's pigeons and came to understand them better.
A narrator describes the dangers that hawks pose to pigeons in Cairo.
A narrator explains how he trained to become a professional pigeon keeper.
A narrator tells of an argument with his mother about climbing walls.
questions.e: The passage follows the narrator from watching the flock to visiting the roof and learning the truth about the white pigeon. The choice about training as a pigeon keeper goes far beyond a single visit.
ce: Right: it covers his watching from the window, his worry about the white pigeon and what Am Ragab teaches him.
Wrong: hawks are mentioned only once, in Am Ragab's explanation.
Wrong: he visits the roof once at the end; no training or career is described.
Wrong: the fall is only the reason he is at home; no argument is described.

questions.q: According to the passage, the narrator spent so much time at the window because he:
c: had been asked to keep watch on the roof opposite.
was afraid to go outside after his fall.
had a broken leg and his friends had stopped visiting.
wanted to become a pigeon keeper like Am Ragab.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, the comparison of Am Ragab moving the pole "like a conductor" mainly serves to:

suggest that the pigeons were frightened of the pole.
suggest that he directed the flock's movements with skill and control.

c: was angry that Am Ragab neglected the white pigeon.

c: shatter into pieces.
interrupt.
lessen.
stop working.
questions.e: "The hour when the heat began to break" is the time of evening when the heat starts to ease. "Shatter into pieces" is the literal meaning and makes no sense for heat.

Right: in the evening, the heat starts to become less intense.

Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about why some jobs pay more than others. The economist, the company and the figures in the table are fictional.

[1] Why does one job pay more than another? The most familiar answers involve skill and training: a surgeon earns more than a hospital porter partly because years of study stand between a school-leaver and the operating theatre. But economists have long recognised a second, less obvious force. In 1776, in The Wealth of Nations, Adam Smith observed that wages vary with how pleasant or unpleasant a job is. Work that is dirty, dangerous, lonely or done at odd hours must, other things being equal, offer more money, or too few people will agree to do it.

[2] Economists call these extra payments compensating differentials: the higher wage compensates the worker for something the job takes away, whether comfort, safety or time with family. The idea is simple, but testing it is surprisingly hard. Unpleasant jobs often differ from pleasant ones in many ways at once — in the skills they require, in where they are located, in who applies for them — and any of these differences might explain a gap in pay.

[3] Economist Nadia Saleh found an unusually clean test inside a single company. The firm, a large food distributor, runs warehouses in which workers do almost exactly the same tasks: unloading lorries, moving pallets and preparing orders. The workers need the same training and are hired from the same towns. Two things, however, vary. Some work by day and some by night, and some work in ordinary warehouses while others work in cold stores kept at about twenty degrees below zero to protect frozen goods. Because the tasks are the same, any difference in pay is likely to reflect the conditions themselves. Saleh's figures are summarised below.

Shift and warehouse | Pay (day shift, ordinary warehouse = 100) | Applicants per vacancy
Day, ordinary | 100 | 9
Night, ordinary | 116 | 4
Day, cold store | 111 | 5
Night, cold store | 129 | 2

[4] The pattern fits Smith's idea closely. Both night work and cold work carried a premium, and the job that combined them paid the most. Just as important, the premiums appeared exactly where the company struggled to find staff. The day jobs in ordinary warehouses attracted many applicants for each opening; the night jobs in the cold stores attracted very few, even at the highest pay. Saleh argues that wages had been pushed upward over the years by the simple need to fill the shifts.

[5] Yet Saleh is careful not to conclude that every hard job pays well. Across the economy as a whole, many of the most unpleasant jobs — cleaning, care work, harvesting crops in summer heat — are also among the worst paid. How can this be, if employers must pay people to accept discomfort?

[6] Her answer is that compensating differentials depend on choice. The theory assumes that workers can compare jobs and turn down the unpleasant ones unless they are paid enough. In the warehouses, this was true: a worker offered a night shift in the cold store could take a day job in an ordinary warehouse instead, or move to a competing firm nearby. Many low-paid workers elsewhere have no such options. If people lack the qualifications, the transport or the legal right to work elsewhere, an employer does not need to pay them extra to put up with hardship; they will accept it anyway.

[7] This makes the idea of compensating differentials less a law of nature than a description of what happens when workers have real alternatives. Where they do, unpleasant work tends to earn a premium. Where they do not, the same discomfort may come with no reward at all. For Saleh, this is the most useful lesson of her study: "If you want to know whether a hard job will be paid fairly, don't just look at the job. Look at the other doors the worker could walk through."

Passage III — Humanities

HUMANITIES: This passage is from an original essay about the art of making sound effects for films. The sound artist described is fictional.

[1] Watch a scene from almost any film with the sound turned off, and something strange happens: the characters seem to float. Their footsteps make no noise, the doors they close are silent, and the cup a woman sets on the table touches it without a sound. Turn the sound back on, and the world becomes solid again. What most viewers never realise is that many of those small sounds were not recorded when the scene was filmed. They were made later, by hand, in a quiet room, by people who watched the scene on a screen and performed it again in sound.

[2] This craft is known as Foley, after Jack Foley, who worked at a Hollywood studio when films first began to talk in the late 1920s. On film sets then, and on many sets ever since, microphones were placed to capture the actors' voices clearly; footsteps, rustling clothes and the clink of cutlery were often too faint, or were lost in the noise of the set. Foley and the artists who followed him found that it was easier to add these sounds afterwards, recording them in time with the picture.

[3] A Foley stage today looks less like a studio than a junk shop. One wall may hold dozens of pairs of shoes; the floor is divided into small patches of gravel, sand, wood, tiles and concrete, so that an artist can walk a character across any surface. Shelves hold bags of keys, old telephones, sheets of metal and boxes of vegetables. Many of the sounds come from unexpected sources. A bunch of celery, twisted and snapped, makes a convincing breaking bone. Footsteps in snow are often produced by squeezing a leather pouch filled with cornflour. The goal is never the real object but the sound the audience expects to hear, which is not always the same thing.

[4] Samia Fawzi, a Foley artist with thirty years of experience, describes her work as a kind of acting. "When I do the footsteps for a character, I have to know who she is," she says. "Is she tired? Is she angry? Is she trying not to wake someone?" A frightened person walks differently from a confident one, and Fawzi adjusts the weight, speed and rhythm of every step to match. She often performs a single character's footsteps from the beginning of a film to the end so that the walk stays consistent, just as an actor keeps the same voice.

[5] The best Foley, she insists, is invisible. Audiences notice sound effects only when something is wrong: a footstep that comes a fraction of a second late, or a punch that sounds too soft for the blow on screen. When everything is right, no one thinks about the sounds at all; they simply believe what they are watching. This is both the pride and the frustration of her profession. "If I do my job perfectly," Fawzi says, "nobody will ever know I was there."

[6] Digital technology has changed the craft but not replaced it. Large libraries of recorded sounds now allow editors to drop in a door slam or a car horn with a few clicks, and for some films this is enough. Yet Foley artists remain in demand, partly because library sounds are, by definition, not made for any particular scene. A recorded footstep cannot know that a character is limping, or that she is carrying a heavy bag, or that she has just heard bad news. Performed sound can.

[7] There is something fitting in the fact that this most invisible art still depends so heavily on the human body. In an industry full of machines, the sound of a person crossing a room is very often made by another person crossing a small square of floor, watching a screen and listening carefully to her own feet.

Passage IV — Natural Science (Paired Passages)

NATURAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an original essay by an astronomer. Passage B is from an original essay by an engineer who designs street lighting for cities. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "Give Us Back the Night"

[1] When my grandmother was a girl, she could lie on the roof of her house on summer nights and see the Milky Way stretched across the sky like a river of light. From the same roof today, on the clearest night of the year, I can count perhaps twenty stars. The sky has not changed. What has changed is the glow rising from the city around us: millions of lamps, signs and windows, much of whose light shines not down onto the streets where it is needed but sideways and upward, where it is scattered by dust and moisture and spread across the whole sky.

[2] Astronomers call this skyglow, and its effects reach far beyond astronomy. Studies of satellite measurements suggest that a large part of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. For professional observatories, the problem is so serious that new telescopes are built on remote mountains, far from large towns, and even there the glow of distant cities can be measured on the horizon.

[3] Nor are we the only ones affected. Many living things depend on the natural cycle of light and dark. On some beaches, newly hatched sea turtles, which find the sea by moving towards the brighter horizon, crawl inland towards the lights of hotels and roads instead. Birds that migrate at night can become confused by brightly lit buildings, circling them until they are exhausted. Insects gather around street lamps in vast numbers, with consequences for the animals that feed on them.

[4] The frustrating thing is that this is the easiest form of pollution to cure. Unlike chemicals in a river, light disappears the moment we switch it off. Every city could cut its skyglow sharply within a year, without leaving anyone in darkness, simply by deciding to light only what needs to be lit. What is missing is not technology but the will to treat the night sky as something worth protecting.

PASSAGE B — "Light Where It Is Needed"

[1] I have spent my career putting light into cities, and I make no apology for it. Good street lighting helps drivers see people crossing the road, helps people find their way home, and allows shops, cafés and markets to stay open after dark. In a hot country, the cooler hours after sunset are when much of public life happens. A dark street is not a neutral thing; for many people, it is a street they will not walk down.

[2] That said, I agree with astronomers on one point: a great deal of the light we produce is wasted. A badly designed lamp that throws light upward or into bedroom windows does nothing for the person on the pavement. It costs money, uses energy and, as my astronomer friends remind me, hides the stars. The solution is not less light but better light. Modern fittings can be shielded so that they shine only downward. Lamps can be dimmed in the quietest hours of the night and brightened again when sensors detect someone approaching.

[3] The arrival of the LED has made this both easier and harder. LEDs use far less electricity than older lamps, and they can be aimed and controlled very precisely. But because they are cheap to run, some cities have simply installed more of them, and brighter ones, than they need. Many early LED street lamps also gave a harsh, bluish-white light, which scatters more in the atmosphere than warmer colours do and appears to disturb wildlife more. Warmer, amber-coloured LEDs are now widely available, and I recommend them wherever they can be used.

[4] Where I part company with some campaigners is in their belief that the problem is simple. Lighting decisions involve safety, cost, local businesses and the wishes of residents, who do not always want their streets dimmed. Change is possible, and it is happening, but it will come one street at a time.

Wrong: mountain observatories are mentioned only as an example of the problem.

Right: paragraphs 1–3 describe the harm, and paragraph 4 says it is "the easiest form of pollution to cure".

It costs money, uses energy and, as my astronomer friends remind me, hides the stars. The solution is not less light but better light. Modern fittings can be shielded so that they shine only downward. Lamps can be dimmed in the quietest hours of the night and brightened again when sensors detect someone approaching.

[3] The arrival of the LED has made this both easier and harder. LEDs use far less electricity than older lamps, and they can be aimed and controlled very precisely. But because they are cheap to run, some cities have simply installed more of them, and brighter ones, than they need. Many early LED street lamps also gave a harsh, bluish-white light, which scatters more in the atmosphere than warmer colours do and appears to disturb wildlife more. Warmer, amber-coloured LEDs are now widely available, and I recommend them wherever they can be used.

[4] Where I part company with some campaigners is in their belief that the problem is simple. Lighting decisions involve safety, cost, local businesses and the wishes of residents, who do not always want their streets dimmed. Change is possible, and it is happening, but it will come one street at a time.
questions.q: Taken together, Passage A's statement that "what is missing is not technology" and Passage B's description of shielded, dimmable lamps suggest that:
c: engineers have no interest in protecting the night sky.
astronomers invented the first shielded street lamps.
most cities have already solved the problem of skyglow.
the tools needed to reduce wasted light are already available.
questions.e: Passage A's claim and Passage B's examples fit together: shielded, dimmable lamps exist now. The choice about engineers is contradicted by Passage B's own recommendations.
ce: Wrong: the engineer recommends shielding and warmer light partly to protect the sky and wildlife.
Wrong: neither passage says who invented shielded lamps.
Wrong: both authors describe skyglow as a continuing problem.
Right: Passage A says technology is not the problem, and Passage B describes that technology.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for EVERY question, including the ones you got right, and check the reason given for each wrong choice.
Sort your wrong answers into Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas. The results screen links each weak skill to a lesson.

Main idea, detail and inference mistakes: go back to "Main Idea and Summary Questions", "Detail Questions: 'According to the Passage'", "Relationships: Sequence, Cause–Effect and Comparison" and "Inference Questions: 'It Can Reasonably Be Inferred'".
Word meaning, purpose and point-of-view mistakes: review "Words and Phrases in Context", "Purpose, Function and Text Structure" and "Point of View, Tone and Perspective".
Paired-passage, table and evidence mistakes: review "Paired Passages: Comparing Two Authors", "Passages with Charts, Tables and Graphs" and "Evaluating Arguments: Claims, Evidence and Reasoning".
If you ran out of time, re-read "ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart" and practise one passage a day with a 10-minute timer.
